The functional boundaries we were familiar with are loosening.  
Junior development: no longer just an executor who types code, but evolves into an operator who can harness AI to write code; mastering Skills and Prompts becomes a new basic skill.  
Senior development: upgraded to Harness Engineer, whose core work is designing AI’s constraints, context, and rules, allowing AI to run efficiently on a controlled track.  
Architect: focus shifts from system design to human-AI collaboration architecture; true judgment lies in deciding “what to hand to AI and what must be controlled by humans.”  
Testing and security engineers: evolve into AI Quality Engineer and AI Security Expert respectively—the former designs test closed loops to verify AI output; the latter builds AI security testing Skills and includes computational security considerations.  
Behind all these changes lies an unchanged core capability: abstract thinking—knowing what to have AI do and how to verify whether AI did it right. This is where engineers’ true irreplaceability lives in the AI era.
9k9k5r:391: For teams that want to introduce AI Coding into high-risk backend systems, building the context system is the top priority. This article provides an actionable progressive path: the first step is to establish a project constitution (Agent.md), whose core principle is "project structure as context, architecture patterns as constraints, inline feedback comments" (line 205). This means the project's directory structure, module boundaries, and calling conventions themselves serve as implicit constraints on AI behavior. The second step is to replace "positive preaching" with "counterexample immunization" (line 207). Every rule should include both a wrong example and a correct example, letting the AI learn "what is wrong" through comparison. This is far more effective than simply telling the AI to "be careful." The third step is to build a reusable pattern library, including CR check patterns, coding pattern libraries, and concurrency design patterns (line 209). These patterns should come from real problems and be A/B-validated, rather than being summarized from subjective experience. The fourth step is to pin domain knowledge locally, including RFC original text, competitor implementations, and open-source code references (line 211). This solves the problem of stale AI training data.

e8mv4z:404: Multi-model, multi-agent adversarial CR is one of the most original engineering innovations in this article. Its core idea (lines 351-387) can be summarized as: using multiple models to independently review in parallel, then cross-validating, to uncover single-model knowledge blind spots, attention blind spots, and confirmation bias. The effectiveness of adversarial CR comes from an insight rooted in information theory: when multiple independent "experts" review the same code, the sets of issues each one misses are often non-overlapping. Through cross-validation, issues discovered by multiple models at the same time have high confidence, while issues found by only a single model need to enter a debate-style discussion stage. This mechanism essentially simulates the cross-review process among human engineers. However, the article also candidly acknowledges its limitation: a false-positive rate as high as 36% (line 465)—that is, among 9 code issues, only 1 is a true P0. This means that although adversarial CR improves defect discovery, it also adds significant review burden. The 36% false-positive rate may be related to the original design intent of adversarial CR—preferring to over-report rather than miss real risks. This is a classic engineering trade-off between "rather cry wolf than miss" and "rather miss than cry wolf."
